How much flood risk is here?

FEMA's National Risk Index rates Collier County's coastal flood risk Very High and inland flood risk Relatively High, from expected annual loss.

  • Coastal flood riskVery High
  • Coastal modeled annual loss (county)$9,409,501/yr (Relatively High, 83rd national percentile)
  • Inland flood riskRelatively High
  • Inland modeled annual loss (county)$123,614,647/yr (Relatively High, 89th national percentile)

Modeled annual loss is FEMA's estimate for the whole county (all buildings), not any one home's expected loss or premium, and not a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Am I required to carry it?

About 79.7% of the NFIP policy units in this dataset for Collier County are in mapped high-risk (A/V) zones — not 79.7% of all buildings. In a Special Flood Hazard Area a federally backed mortgage legally requires flood insurance.

  • Zone AE65,039 policy units
  • Zone X20,359 policy units
  • Zone AH13,279 policy units
  • Zone VE1,125 policy units
  • Zone AHB482 policy units
  • Zone A11 policy units
  • Zone AO4 policy units
  • Zone D2 policy units
  • Other or unclassified zones1 policy units

Zone mix by policy units (summed policyCount). Federal rule: a lender must require flood insurance on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area with a federally backed loan (42 U.S.C. §4012a). This is the mix of existing policies, not of all buildings, and does not establish any one property's obligation.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How much does it cost here?

Among existing single-family primary-residence NFIP policies in Collier County, the median annual cost is $1,265, with the middle half between $991 and $1,869 (31,802 policies). This is what current policyholders pay — a new policy on a different building can differ.

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus fees), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half (p25–p75); the orange line is FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $23,174,312,000 of building and $3,578,545,000 of contents coverage across all Collier County policies.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

76.9% of 31,802 single-family policies pay less than FEMA's own full-risk price; the median full-risk premium is $2,739 versus the $1,265 actually charged.

  • Median charged now$1,265
  • Median full-risk price$2,739
  • Pay below full risk76.9% of 31,802

Years to the full-risk price: under the statutory cap, premiums for most primary residences rise at most 18% a year (HFIAA cap, FEMA Risk Rating 2.0). At that maximum rate a policy at today's median ($1,265) would take at least about 5 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk price ($2,739). This is the cap on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy; statutory surcharges and fees are outside the cap.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Can I pay less than the sticker price?

4 of Collier County's 4 NFIP communities carry a Community Rating System discount that cuts every eligible policy's premium — up to 25% inside the high-risk zone (Collier County).

CommunityCRS classHigh-risk discountOther-area discount
Collier County525%10%
Marco Island, City Of525%10%
Naples, City Of525%10%
Everglades City, City Of95%5%

The Community Rating System cuts NFIP premiums for every eligible policy in a community that does extra flood work. The discount shown is the community's rate; what share of its policies currently receive it is not in this data. Confirm with your agent.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective October 22, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Between 1978 and 2026, Collier County had 14,773 paid NFIP flood claims totalling $1,125,379,093.

Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2022 ($920,755,911), 2024 ($129,179,309), 2017 ($60,935,239). Net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 14,773 paid claims since 1978 against 100,302 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How common is flood insurance here?

Collier County has about 42.7 NFIP flood policies for every 100 homes (100,302 policy units vs 234,732 housing units).

  • NFIP policy units100,302
  • Housing units234,732
  • Policies per 100 homes42.7

A coverage-commonness proxy: policy units include some multi-unit and non-residential policies and exclude private flood insurance, so read it as how widespread NFIP coverage is here, not an exact share of households.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP + U.S. Census ACS 5-year 2023 (B25001), retrieved October 22, 2026.

How often is this county a flood disaster?

Collier County has had 29 distinct federal flood, hurricane or tropical-storm disaster declarations. The most recent:

  • 2024 — Hurricane: Hurricane Milton
  • 2024 — Hurricane: Hurricane Helene
  • 2024 — Tropical Storm: Hurricane Debby
  • 2023 — Hurricane: Hurricane Idalia
  • 2022 — Hurricane: Hurricane Nicole
  • 2022 — Hurricane: Hurricane Ian

Distinct storms by calendar year (one storm's emergency and major-disaster declarations are counted once), not individual declaration records.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective declarations through 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

More data: FEMA disaster aid & reconciliation

Did the government pay homeowners after floods?

FEMA approved $78,142,559 in Individual & Households housing help to Collier County homeowners across 8 disasters, on 75,311 valid registrations.

FEMA Individual Assistance is disaster aid, usually capped and partial — separate from NFIP insurance and not a substitute for a policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective owner registrations by disaster; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our counts are checked against FEMA's official figure and the API's own totals.

In-force count: 100,302 policy units (from 56,214 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). FEMA official reconciliation count pending for this county. Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 56214/56214 fetched; claims: 14773/14773 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why premiums are rising — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
